title: In MR the player sees the real place, only the floor is replaced
text: Quest 3 passthrough shows the real walls, people, sky and light; the engine only swaps the floor for the Land's ground and stands models on it at 1:1 scale. Design every option as a layer on top of a real place, not as a sealed virtual world. Ask what is around the floor, because that is half of what the player will see.
use_when: Any MR brief, before proposing themes or scenery.
do: Ask what surrounds the floor (walls, windows, sky, trees, people)
Describe in environment_fit what the player sees beyond the floor
avoid: Promising a fully enclosed fantasy world in MR
Ignoring the real ceiling or sky in the key art prompt
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Everything stands at real 1:1 scale on the real floor
text: A 1 m model in the Land is 1 m tall in the room, next to real furniture and people. A 4 m dragon in a 3 m high living room clips through the ceiling visually, while the same dragon on a car park looks huge and right. Size hero pieces against the real ceiling height and the floor size, not against an imagined world.
use_when: Choosing hero pieces and prop sizes for an indoor or small venue.
do: Keep indoor hero pieces under about 2.5 m tall unless the ceiling is high
Use tall pieces outdoors or in halls
avoid: Huge models in low rooms
Tiny props in a 20 m car park where they disappear
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Use the real walls as the edge of the world
text: Players can see the real walls, so make them part of the fiction: the fortress wall, the edge of the island, the end of the map. Place the route so it turns before the walls with at least 0.6 m to spare, and put low edge scenery near the walls so the change from virtual floor to real wall feels intended.
use_when: Indoor venues with visible walls on most sides.
do: Name the walls in the story (the castle wall, the ice cliff)
Line the edges with low scenery that frames the real wall
avoid: Routes that point players straight at a wall at speed
Fighting the walls with scenery that pretends they are not there

see_also.why: Meta's mixed reality guidelines discuss room boundaries and real walls, which the card turns into deliberate world edges.

title: A real skyline or garden becomes the backdrop for free
text: On a rooftop, car park or garden the real sky, trees and buildings fill the view above the floor. Pick themes that agree with them: a city skyline suits sci-fi or heroes, trees suit forest, dinosaurs or farm, open sky suits pirates or islands. Put the finish portal so players face the best view when they arrive.
use_when: Outdoor venues with a visible horizon.
do: Match the theme to what is on the horizon
Face the finish towards the best real view
avoid: Space or underwater themes in bright midday outdoors
Facing the finish at a blank wall or a parked car

title: Turn the real crowd into the in-game audience
text: In a hall or at an event, the people standing around are visible in passthrough. Frame them as the arena audience, the villagers or the race fans. The story can say the crowd is watching your trial, which makes cheers feel part of the game and makes players perform for them.
use_when: Events, halls and booths where spectators stand around the play area.
do: Mention the watching crowd in the intro story
Put the finish facing the spectators
avoid: Stories where the player is alone in an empty world while 30 people are visible
Asking the crowd to do in-game tasks

see_also.why: Designing the Spectator Experience directly addresses how spectators and visible performance shape play in public settings.

title: The void floor is dramatic but makes people dizzy
text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop with scenery below. It is a strong wow moment but triggers fear of heights, slower walking and discomfort, especially for first-time VR players and seniors. Use it for short, slow sections with confident adults, never for kids or races.
use_when: When a creator asks for heights, sky islands or falling scenery.
do: Offer it only for adults or experienced players
Keep the route short and slow when the void is on
Warn on the intro card
avoid: Void floor in races or timed runs
Void floor for kids 6-9, seniors or first-time VR
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Mark backdrop pieces VR only so they vanish in MR
text: Decor can be flagged VR only so it is hidden in MR and shown only in full VR. Use it for walls, ceilings, skies and tall backdrops that would otherwise float through the real room or block the view of real walls and people. Floor-level scenery stays visible on both.
use_when: A Land that will be played both in MR and in full VR.
do: Flag backdrop walls and ceiling pieces VR only
Keep floor-level scenery visible in MR
avoid: Tall backdrops that overlap real walls in MR

title: There is no joystick movement in MR, the route must fit the real floor
text: In MR players move only by walking, so the whole route, every checkpoint and the portal must lie inside the real empty floor. A creator who wants a long journey gets it through loops, zig-zags and story labels, not distance. Offer a spiral or out-and-back route instead of teleporting or scrolling worlds.
use_when: When the creator imagines a big world or a long trip in a small space.
do: Use loops, spirals or zig-zags to lengthen the walk
Make each checkpoint label a new place in the story
avoid: Promising teleport, flying or joystick movement in MR
Routes longer than the floor allows

title: Living room: small, furniture, 1-2 players
text: A typical cleared living room gives 3 x 3 to 4 x 5 m of floor, with sofas, tables and a TV at the edges and warm indoor light. It fits 1-2 players, a short loop of 4-5 checkpoints and small props. Family members watch from the sofa. Cosy themes (toys, candy, farm, small dragons) fit better than epic battles.
use_when: The creator plays at home.
do: Ask them to measure the empty floor after pushing furniture back
Use small props and a short loop
Make the sofa side the audience side
avoid: Races or 4 players at once
Routes that pass within 0.6 m of a glass table

title: Classroom: desks to move, a class watching
text: A classroom is about 7 x 8 m but desks fill it; after pushing them aside the clear floor is often 4 x 6 m. Light is steady fluorescent, good for colour. 1-3 students play while 25-35 watch, so turn taking and spectator moments matter more than length. Learning themes (Thai history, planets, animals) with checkpoint labels as facts work well.
use_when: A teacher or school group plans to play in a classroom.
do: Ask for the clear floor after desks move, not the room size
Keep plays to 2-3 minutes so the whole class gets a turn
Use checkpoint labels as short facts
avoid: Long solo plays while 30 students wait
Assuming the whole room is empty

title: Hall or function room: big, indoor, good for groups
text: A school or hotel hall often gives 12 x 20 m or more of clear floor with steady light and sometimes a stage. It supports races of up to 6 players, long routes and two lanes. Lights can often be dimmed, which makes spooky and neon themes possible. Spectators stand along the sides or sit on the stage.
use_when: Events in a school hall, hotel ballroom or community hall.
do: Ask whether lights can be dimmed
Plan two lanes or a race
Put the finish in front of the stage or seating
avoid: Using only a small corner of a big hall
Routes that cross the doors people walk through

title: Sports hall or gym: court lines, echo, wide floor
text: A gym or futsal court gives 15 x 25 m or more of flat floor with painted lines. Light is bright and even. Basketball hoops and wall bars stand at the edges, and benches give spectators a clear view. It suits races, sports or hero themes and long routes.
use_when: Playing in a school gym, sports hall or covered court.
do: Use the court lines to align lanes
Seat spectators on the benches along one long side
avoid: Routes under hoops or near wall bars
Ignoring the echo when planning loud spectator moments

title: Garden or lawn: daylight, trees, uneven ground
text: A garden offers 5 x 8 m up to large lawns, but grass is uneven, there are trees, paths and garden furniture, and daylight washes out glow. Players walk slower on grass. Bright themes (farm, dinosaurs, pirates, candy) fit; dark or neon themes do not. Trees inside the floor must be listed as obstacles and the route kept away from them.
use_when: Outdoor play in a garden, park or school field.
do: Ask about trees, slopes, holes and sprinklers
Use noon or morning lighting
Choose bright, saturated themes
avoid: Spooky or neon themes at midday
Hazards that need quick steps on wet grass

title: Car park: huge and flat, but traffic and sun
text: An empty car park gives 20 x 30 m or more of flat hard floor, ideal for long routes, two lanes and 6-player races. The risks are cars, kerbs, drains, strong sun and heat. Only use it when it is closed to traffic. Big hero pieces read well against open sky.
use_when: Large outdoor events or tests in a car park.
do: Confirm it is closed to cars and fenced or staffed
Keep routes off kerbs and drains
Play in the evening or in shade for comfort
avoid: Assuming the whole car park is safe
Dark themes in midday sun

title: Rooftop: skyline view, wind and edges
text: A rooftop gives a dramatic city skyline but has parapets, vents, wind and sun. Keep the route at least 2 m from any roof edge or low railing, much more than the usual 0.6 m, because a player stepping back cannot see what is behind. Sci-fi, heroes or night city themes work best in the evening.
use_when: The creator wants to play on a building rooftop.
do: Keep 2 m or more from roof edges and railings
Use evening or night lighting for city themes
Face the finish at the skyline
avoid: Void floor on a rooftop
Hazards that push players backwards towards an edge

title: Mall atrium: crowds, bright light, passers-by
text: A mall atrium offers about 8 x 12 m with bright mixed light, shiny floors, escalators and a constant crowd of passers-by. It is good for brand events and showing off, but people may walk into the area. Put a barrier or staff around it, keep plays short (2-3 minutes) and design big visible moments for the crowd.
use_when: Promotional events in shopping malls.
do: Ask for a barrier or rope around the floor
Keep plays to 2-3 minutes
Put the leaderboard screen facing the walkway
avoid: Dark themes under skylights
Long plays with a queue of shoppers

title: Event booth: 3 x 3 to 6 x 6 m and a fast queue
text: Exhibition booths usually give 3 x 3, 3 x 6 or 6 x 6 m of floor with strong show lighting and noise. Most players are first-time VR and want a quick taste, so 90 seconds to 3 minutes per play with a clear goal works best. The booth lives on throughput and on how fun it looks from the aisle.
use_when: Trade shows, game shows and expos.
do: Design for 2-3 minute plays
Face the key moments to the aisle
Plan queue entertainment on a screen
avoid: 5 minute plays that stall the queue
Routes that cross the booth entrance

title: Fortal court: 14 x 22 m, steady light, 2-6 players
text: The Fortal court (XR Arena, Chiang Mai) is an indoor 14 x 22 m floor with walls on all sides, painted court lines, 4 doors along one long wall and steady indoor light. Staff and families watch along one long side and a wall screen can show the leaderboard. It fits long routes, races, two lanes and spooky or neon themes.
use_when: The creator plays at the Fortal court (venue fortal-court).
do: Use the preset instead of asking for size
Put key moments along the spectator long side
Show the race leaderboard on the wall screen
avoid: Routes through the doors on the long wall
Asking the creator to measure the court

title: Under 3 x 3 m only the runner genre fits
text: If either side of the MR space is under 3 m, battle and tactics do not fit: enemies need room to walk in from the edges and the 6 x 8 board needs squares a person can step on. All 3 options must then be runners that differ in theme, route and feeling instead. The builder checks this.
use_when: MR brief with width or depth below 3 m.
do: Make all 3 options runners with different loops and moods
Use 3-4 checkpoints
avoid: Proposing battle or tactics in a 2 x 3 m room

title: Under 4 x 4 m: 1-2 players, a short loop, no race
text: A floor under 4 x 4 m is a small play area: plan 1-2 players, a short loop of 4-5 checkpoints and small props. A live race needs parallel space and does not fit, so offer a solo time attack with a leaderboard instead. From about 3.7 m on the shortest side the builder's small rules apply (3-6 checkpoints, 1.2-4 m between stops, 8-30 objects); below that the tiny-room rules take over.
use_when: Small MR floors such as a living room or booth.
do: Plan a loop or figure-eight of 4-5 checkpoints
Offer a solo time attack instead of a race
avoid: Live races with 3 or more players
Big hero pieces that eat the floor

title: 4 x 4 to 10 x 10 m: 1-4 players, loops and zig-zags
text: Medium floors such as a cleared classroom or a small hall fit 1-4 players, loops or zig-zags and 5-7 checkpoints. When the usable side is 5-10 m the builder expects 1.8-6 m between stops, a 1.2 m clear circle around the spawn and 15-50 objects. Shared floor play works well with 2-3 players.
use_when: Medium MR floors.
do: Use 5-7 checkpoints 1.8-6 m apart
Pick loop or zig-zag routes
avoid: Two-lane races under 8 m wide
Checkpoints closer than 1.8 m

title: Over 10 x 10 m: up to 6 players, long routes, races
text: When the usable side is 10 m or more (for example the 14 x 22 m Fortal court) the builder uses large rules: 4-10 checkpoints 2.5-9 m apart, a 1.5 m clear circle around the spawn and 20-80 objects. This is where races, two lanes and hub-and-spoke routes shine. Fill the space with 3-12 vignettes so long walks do not feel empty.
use_when: Halls, courts, gyms and car parks.
do: Use 7-10 checkpoints 2.5-9 m apart
Offer races or two lanes
Place vignettes along the longer legs
avoid: Huddling a short loop in one corner
Stops more than 9 m apart with nothing between

title: Judge size by the shortest side minus 1.2 m
text: The builder measures the usable floor as the shortest side minus 0.6 m on each edge. A 4 x 8 m space is really 2.8 m usable, which counts as small, not medium. Always reason from the shortest side, because the route must turn inside it.
use_when: Any time a size rule is applied.
do: Subtract 1.2 m from the shortest side before choosing rules
Mention the usable size in environment_fit
avoid: Using the long side or the area to pick a size class

title: A shortest side under 3.7 m triggers the tiny-room rules
text: The builder subtracts the 0.6 m edge margin on both sides, so any floor whose shortest side is under about 3.7 m has less than 2.5 m usable and gets tiny rules: 3-4 checkpoints, stops spaced about 45 percent of the usable side (at least 0.5 m), hazard radius 0.35 m, a 0.6 m spawn circle, 2-4 vignettes and 8-20 objects. A 3.5 x 5 m bedroom is tiny, not small. Plan a tight circuit where the story labels and one hero piece carry the experience.
use_when: The shortest side of the MR floor is between 2 and 3.7 m.
do: Check the shortest side against 3.7 m before choosing a checkpoint count
Plan 3-4 checkpoints in a tight circle around one hero piece
avoid: Planning 5 or more checkpoints for a 3 x 4 m room
Hazards that force side steps toward furniture

title: Keep everything at least 0.6 m from the edge of the floor
text: Players overshoot targets, swing arms and step backwards. Keep checkpoints, hazards, the portal and the route at least 0.6 m inside the edge of the measured floor, and more next to glass, stairs or roof edges. The builder applies 0.6 m by default.
use_when: Placing any marker in MR.
do: Treat the outer 0.6 m as a no-go strip
Add extra margin near glass, stairs and drops
avoid: Checkpoints on the edge of the floor
Hazards that make players step outward
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Keep a 1.2 m corridor clear along the walking route
text: Players walk the straight lines from spawn through the checkpoints in order to the portal. No object may stand within 0.6 m plus half its footprint of those lines, which gives a 1.2 m corridor. Arches and gates can sit on the line only if marked walkThrough. This keeps players from flinching at virtual props they think are solid.
use_when: Dressing the route with scenery.
do: Line props along the sides of the corridor
Use walkThrough arches to frame the path
avoid: Rocks or trees on the walking line
Narrow gaps between props players must squeeze through

title: Real obstacles inside the floor must stay off the route
text: A pillar, tree or table inside the floor is a real thing players can hit. List it in obstacles, keep the route and markers well away from it (at least 0.6 m plus a margin) and consider dressing it with a virtual piece of the same footprint, such as a rock around a pillar, so it reads as part of the world.
use_when: The creator mentions a pillar, tree, table or other fixed object.
do: Ask for each obstacle and roughly where it is
Route around it and dress it as a landmark
avoid: Placing a checkpoint beside a pillar
Pretending the obstacle is not there
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Convert paces to metres: 1 pace is about 0.75 m
text: Many creators do not know the size in metres. Ask them to walk the empty floor and count normal steps: 1 adult pace is about 0.75 m (a child's pace is shorter, about 0.5 m). 6 paces by 8 paces is about 4.5 x 6 m. Round down, never up.
use_when: The creator does not know the floor size in metres.
do: Offer count your steps as a quick-reply choice
Round the result down to the nearest half metre
avoid: Rounding up
Using a child's step count with the adult conversion

title: If the size is unknown, assume a small floor and say so
text: If the creator cannot give the size even in paces, assume the safe case: a 3 x 3 m floor indoors, 1-2 players, a short loop. Write the assumption into the brief and tell the creator the game can scale up if they later measure a bigger space. Guessing big risks routes that run into walls.
use_when: The creator does not know or skips the size question.
do: Assume 3 x 3 m indoors
Write the assumption into the brief
Ask once more with paces as an option
avoid: Guessing a large floor
Finishing the interview without any size for a space venue

title: Ask for the empty floor, not the room
text: Rooms include furniture; the play area is only the floor that is clear. Ask how big the empty floor you can walk on is, and offer quick choices such as about 3 x 3 m, 5 x 5 m, 10 x 10 m or bigger, and I will count my steps. The answer changes genre, player count and route, so it is required for a space venue.
use_when: Interview step about the environment.
do: Offer 4-5 size choices plus a paces option
Explain in why that size decides how many can play
avoid: Asking for room size only
Skipping the size question

title: Space checkpoints so players walk, not shuffle
text: Stops too close together make players shuffle in place; too far apart and the walk feels empty. The builder checks 1.2-4 m between stops on small floors, 1.8-6 m on medium and 2.5-9 m on large. Aim for the middle of the range and vary it so the route has rhythm.
use_when: Placing checkpoints in the layout brief.
do: Aim for the middle of the spacing range
Alternate a short and a long leg
avoid: Equal spacing everywhere
Several stops at the minimum distance in a row

title: Hazards sit on the route but leave room to step around
text: Hazards are red circles that send the player back to the last checkpoint. In MR the player must see them early and step around them without leaving the corridor. Keep hazards at least the builder's gap from each other (0.4 m small, 0.7 m medium, 1 m large floors) and away from the edge, so the dodge is never toward a wall.
use_when: Adding hazards to an MR route.
do: Place hazards where the dodge is toward open floor
Give 2-3 m of sight line before each hazard
avoid: Hazards just after a sharp turn
Hazards that force a step into the edge margin

title: Keep the spawn clear so players start calmly
text: Players put the headset on at the spawn and take a moment to adjust. The builder keeps a clear circle around it: 0.8 m on small floors, 1.2 m medium, 1.5 m large. Put the spawn near the entrance and the staff side so helpers can reach players quickly.
use_when: Choosing where the spawn goes.
do: Put the spawn near the staff and entrance
Face the spawn toward the first checkpoint
avoid: Spawning players facing a wall
Props inside the spawn circle

title: Bright daylight washes out glow and dark themes
text: In sun, passthrough is bright and virtual glow, neon and dark colours look faded. Outdoors in daylight choose bright, saturated themes with strong silhouettes and the noon or morning preset. Save spooky and neon for indoors or after dark.
use_when: Outdoor or window-lit venues in daytime.
do: Pick noon or morning lighting
Use bold colours and big shapes
avoid: Neon or spooky themes at midday
Small glowing markers as the only cue
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Steady indoor light keeps colours readable
text: Halls, classrooms and the Fortal court have even artificial light, so most themes read well. The studio or default presets match it; spooky and neon work if the room lights can be dimmed. Ask whether the lights can be changed, because it opens darker themes.
use_when: Indoor venues.
do: Ask whether lights can be dimmed
Use studio or default when the lights stay on
avoid: Assuming a dark room the venue cannot provide

title: After dark, spooky, neon and night presets shine
text: Outdoors after sunset or in a dimmed hall, glow and dark palettes pop and spooky or neon themes feel strong. But passthrough gets grainy in low light and players see real obstacles less well, so keep some room light on, widen clearances and slow the pace.
use_when: Night events, evening outdoor play or dimmed halls.
do: Use night, spooky or neon presets
Keep some real light so tracking and safety work
Widen corridors and slow the route
avoid: Pitch dark rooms where tracking fails
Fast timed routes at night
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Default lighting preset by venue
text: Garden or car park at midday: noon. Morning outdoor events: morning. Sunset rooftop or garden: evening. Living room or classroom with lights on: default or studio. Hall or court with dimmable lights: spooky or neon for dark themes, studio otherwise. Outdoors after dark: night. Pick the preset that agrees with the real light the player will see.
use_when: Choosing the lighting field in options or build.
do: Match the preset to the real light and time
Explain the pick in environment_fit
avoid: Night preset in a sunlit garden
Noon preset in a dim hall

title: Ask when it will be played, not only where
text: The same garden is a bright dino park at 11:00 and a ghost trail at 19:00. Ask the time of day for any venue with windows or open sky; it decides the lighting preset and which themes are possible. Offer quick choices: morning, midday, evening, night, indoors without windows.
use_when: Interview, outdoor or window-lit venues.
do: Ask time of day together with indoor or outdoor
Record it in time_of_day
avoid: Choosing a dark theme before knowing the time

title: Sun patches from windows fade colours on part of the route
text: A room can have even light except where sunlight falls through a window, and that patch moves over the day. Inside it, virtual colours and hazard circles fade while the rest of the route looks fine, so a player can walk into a hazard they did not see. Ask where the sun falls at play time and keep hazards and checkpoints out of that patch, or close the curtains.
use_when: Indoor venues with large windows, especially east or west facing.
do: Ask where direct sun falls at the planned time
Keep hazards out of sunlit patches
avoid: A hazard right in a sunbeam
Assuming the light at the test visit matches the event time
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Design for walking, never running
text: Players in headsets misjudge real distances and may miss small real objects. Time limits and races must be beatable at a brisk walk. In battle the player steps out of rings, never sprints. Write walk, do not run into the rules of every race.
use_when: Any timed, race or battle design in MR.
do: Set time limits a walking player can beat
Add walk, do not run to the rules
avoid: Time limits that need sprinting
Hazards that need a jump or lunge
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: No sudden scares that make people run
text: A jump scare makes people step back or bolt, and in MR that can mean a wall or a person. Build horror with slow dread: dim light, Thai ghost scenery seen from far away, story labels. Keep scary pieces beside the route and visible early, never popping up in front of a player.
use_when: Spooky or horror themes.
do: Use slow reveals and atmosphere
Place scary models beside the path, visible early
avoid: Monsters appearing right in front of the player
Scares near walls or edges
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: No tasks that need looking up while walking fast
text: Looking up while walking hides the floor and real obstacles and causes trips. Put checkpoint labels and targets at chest to eye height. Tall scenery is fine to admire while standing still at a checkpoint.
use_when: Placing labels, targets and hero pieces.
do: Keep interactive things between knee and eye height
Put tall wow pieces near stops, not mid-leg
avoid: Targets high above the route
Labels that must be read while looking up
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Offer a seated or standing-still way to play
text: Some players cannot or should not walk around: limited mobility, some seniors, a tiny room. The PC platform serves seated players, and in MR battle the player mostly stands in place and steps out of rings. Mention the alternative so the creator can include everyone.
use_when: Players with limited mobility or very small spaces.
do: Suggest the PC version for seated players
Keep MR battle steps small
avoid: Designs that assume everyone can walk 50 m
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Avoid motion sickness: the floor must stay still
text: In MR the player walks for real, so the main sickness risks are a bottomless floor and anything that moves the world instead of the player. Keep the floor stable, avoid the void floor for sensitive players, and use animated rides as scenery, never as something players stand on. Fast spins to find the next checkpoint also cause discomfort, so keep the next stop roughly ahead.
use_when: Constraints mention motion sickness, or players are new to VR.
do: Keep the next checkpoint within a 90 degree turn
Use animated rides as scenery only
avoid: Void floor for sensitive players
Routes with many 180 degree turns
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Default session length: about 4 minutes in MR
text: Most MR walking plays feel complete in 3-5 minutes and stay comfortable. First-time players and events want 2-3 minutes; a home game with keen adults can run 8-10 minutes across chapters. If the creator does not say, use 4 minutes and write it into the brief.
use_when: Session length is unknown.
do: Default to 4 minutes
Use 2-3 minutes for events and young kids
avoid: 15 minute single plays in a headset
No time cap at a queue event
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Plan rest breaks between chapters for long sessions
text: Heat, headset weight and eye strain build up over time, faster in warm venues. If the whole experience runs over 10 minutes, split it into chapters of 3-4 minutes with a short break in which the player can lift the headset or sit down. In battle, the chapter by chapter structure gives natural break points before the boss; in runner, the intro card of a second Land can act as one.
use_when: The creator wants a long session or repeated plays by the same person.
do: Add a break after every 3-4 minute chapter
Put the hardest part right after a break, not at the end of a long stretch
avoid: One continuous 20 minute play
A boss fight after 12 minutes without a break
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Quest 3 is heavy for small children: keep their plays short
text: The headset weighs around half a kilo, which is a lot for a young child's neck, and the fit is loose on small faces. For kids 6-9 keep plays to 2-3 minutes, avoid long periods of looking down, and have a helper adjust the strap. Check the manufacturer's age guidance for the venue.
use_when: Players include young children.
do: Cap plays at 2-3 minutes for under-10s
Plan an adult helper per child
avoid: 10 minute plays for 6 year olds
Designs that need long head tilts
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: At events plan hygiene and turnover between players
text: Each change of player needs wiping the face pad, fitting the strap and a short briefing, about 60-90 seconds. Plan the play length and throughput around it. Disposable face covers and a second headset that alternates keep the queue moving.
use_when: Public events with many players.
do: Budget 60-90 s between players
Suggest two headsets that alternate
avoid: Forgetting changeover time in throughput estimates

title: Hot outdoor venues overheat players and headsets
text: In midday Thai sun, headsets overheat and players sweat into the face pad, and sunlight falling into the lenses can damage the screens. Prefer shade, morning or evening times, and outdoor plays of 2-3 minutes. Store headsets lens-down in the shade between players.
use_when: Outdoor daytime venues in hot weather.
do: Suggest shade or morning or evening play
Shorten outdoor plays to 2-3 minutes
avoid: Long midday sessions in direct sun
Leaving headsets lens-up in the sun
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Draw the headset boundary on the floor that was measured
text: The game only knows the size the creator gave; on site, the safety net is the boundary drawn in the headset. Tell the creator to clear the floor first, then draw the boundary on that same floor, so the Land, its 0.6 m margin and the boundary all match. If the drawn boundary is smaller than the brief, rebuild with the smaller size rather than playing past it.
use_when: Before the first play at a new venue.
do: Clear the floor, then draw the boundary
Rebuild if the boundary is smaller than the brief
avoid: Playing a Land bigger than the drawn boundary
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: One spotter watches the floor during group plays
text: On a shared floor players see each other's avatars but still misjudge distance, and real people may wander in. One staff member or parent stands at the edge with a clear view of the whole floor, ready to call stop. Design routes that flow in one direction so players never walk toward each other head-on.
use_when: Shared floor play or events with several players at once.
do: Plan one spotter per floor at the edge
Make routes flow in one direction
avoid: Routes where two players cross head-on
Spotters standing inside the play area

see_also.why: Meta's safety guidance covers play area supervision and adult oversight, matching the card's spotter role for group play.

title: Kids 6-9: short, bright, forgiving, few words
text: Young children read slowly, scare easily and tire fast. Use 2-3 minute plays, 4-6 checkpoints with labels of 2-4 words, few hazards, no time limit or a generous one, bright high-contrast colours and friendly themes (animals, candy, toys). In tactics use slow guards (4 s or more) or a board with one guard.
use_when: Players are young children.
do: Labels of 2-4 words
Generous or no time limit
Bright, friendly themes
avoid: Spooky themes
Long intro text
Void floor

title: Kids 10-12: give real challenge and a score to beat
text: Older children want to win and to beat their friends. They read short sentences, handle hazards and a time limit, and love leaderboards. Mild spooky themes such as cute Thai ghosts work. Keep plays 3-4 minutes and let the challenge rise across checkpoints.
use_when: Players are 10-12 years old, for example a school class.
do: Add a time limit and a leaderboard
Raise hazard density toward the end
avoid: Babyish themes
Real horror

title: Teens: competition, style and showing off
text: Teens care about looking cool to the friends watching and beating each other. Races, leaderboards, neon and hero themes, tactics guards at 3 s and battle bosses fit. Keep text short and let them restart quickly.
use_when: Players are teenagers.
do: Offer a race or leaderboard
Use bold neon or hero themes
avoid: Childish story text
Slow tutorials

title: Adults at home or with friends: longer, harder, a bit of nostalgia
text: Adults who choose to play (a game night, a team outing, a birthday) are past the novelty and want a real game: 6-10 minutes across chapters, a time limit that bites, a leaderboard among friends. Themes that call back to childhood (pirates, dinosaurs, toys) or local legends land well. They are self-conscious in front of colleagues, so avoid poses or moves that look silly and let the competition be the show.
use_when: Adult players who have tried VR before or play for a social occasion.
do: Offer chapters and a tight time limit
Use nostalgic or local-legend themes
avoid: Childish story text
Moves that make adults look silly in front of colleagues

title: Seniors: steady floor, slow pace, large clear text
text: Older players may have balance or vision limits. Keep the floor stable (no void), no time limit or a generous one, wide corridors, large high-contrast labels and calm themes (temples, gardens, history). Offer the PC version for anyone unsteady on their feet.
use_when: Players include seniors or grandparents.
do: No void floor, no time pressure
Large high-contrast labels
Offer a seated alternative
avoid: Fast hazards
Low-contrast dark themes
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Mixed-age families: one route, two levels of challenge
text: A family group can have a 6 year old and a grandparent at once. Design for the youngest: short, bright, safe. Older players chase the time bonus and avoid hazard penalties while kids simply finish. Shared floor play lets a parent walk beside a child.
use_when: Family groups with mixed ages.
do: Shared floor so a parent can walk beside the child
Speed bonus as an optional challenge
avoid: Difficulty tuned for teens
Scary themes

title: First-time VR players need a calm first minute
text: First-timers spend the first 30-60 seconds looking around and checking that the floor is really there. Put the first checkpoint close and in plain view, no hazards before it, and save the wow for the second half. Keep the intro card to 2 sentences.
use_when: Events or briefs where most players have never used VR.
do: First checkpoint 2-3 m ahead in plain view
No hazard before checkpoint 2
avoid: Tight time limits from the start
Void floor
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Experienced gamers want depth and mastery
text: Players used to VR or games read the rules fast and look for mastery. Give tighter time limits, denser hazards, tactics boards with 3 s guards and a strict capture order, or battle chapters mixing shield and beast enemies with rain. The leaderboard keeps them replaying.
use_when: Players are gamers or VR regulars.
do: Tighter limits and more hazards
A leaderboard for replay
avoid: Long tutorials
Only easy content

title: School classes: many turns, everyone watches
text: With 30 students and 1-2 headsets, the game is mostly watched. Plays of about 2 minutes, a class leaderboard on a projector and checkpoint labels that teach a fact give the watchers a role: they learn and cheer. Use team names so turns feel fair and no personal data is shown.
use_when: Classroom or school event briefs.
do: 2 minute plays
Leaderboard on the projector
Facts as checkpoint labels
avoid: 5 minute plays
Student names on the leaderboard (use team names)

title: Tourists: local culture, little text, quick to understand
text: Tourists may not read Thai and often play only once. Use visual storytelling and very short labels, Thai temples, ghosts or local legends as scenery, and a 2-3 minute play. The experience should be photo worthy for the friends watching.
use_when: Tourist venues or visitors from abroad.
do: Minimal text, strong visuals
Local culture themes
avoid: Long story cards
Jokes that depend on the language

title: Limited mobility: smaller loops, no stepping tasks, or PC
text: For wheelchair users or people who cannot walk far, long MR routes and battle ring dodges exclude them. Offer the PC platform, or a small runner loop with wide flat corridors of 1.5 m and no hazards that need side steps. Ask what they need without asking for medical details.
use_when: The brief mentions wheelchairs, injuries or limited mobility.
do: Offer the PC version
Wide corridors and no hazard steps
avoid: Asking for medical details
Ring dodges as the only mechanic
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Keep in-headset text short: labels under 5 words
text: Text in a headset is harder to read than on a phone, and walking players only glance at it. Keep checkpoint labels to 2-5 words, the goal to one line and the story card to 2-4 short sentences. Young players and tourists need even less.
use_when: Writing labels, goals and story text.
do: Labels of 2-5 words
Story of 2-4 sentences
avoid: Paragraph labels
Rules lists over 4 items

title: High contrast colours for markers, more for kids and seniors
text: Markers must read against both the virtual floor and the real light. Hazards are red, so keep the floor palette away from red and orange. Pair light floors with dark props or the reverse, and avoid low-contrast palettes for kids, seniors and daylight venues.
use_when: Choosing the palette and floor theme.
do: Keep the floor away from red tones
Check the palette for daylight readability
avoid: Red or orange floors that hide hazards
Grey on grey palettes

title: Tactics guard beat by player: 4-5 s for kids, 3 s for gamers
text: In tactics guards move every 3 s or slower. Walking onto a square in MR takes time, so for kids, seniors and first-timers use 4-5 s per beat and few guards; gamers and teens can handle 3 s. A beat that is too fast turns planning into panic and tempts people to rush.
use_when: Designing tactics boards in MR.
do: Slow the beat for young or new players
Use fewer guards on the first board
avoid: Beats under 3 s
Many guards on the first board

title: Set time limits from walking speed and player type
text: Estimate the walk: a brisk adult covers about 1 m per second plus a few seconds at each checkpoint. Give kids and first-timers about double that walking time, adults 1.5 times, gamers 1.2 times. Or leave the limit off and let the time bonus reward speed.
use_when: Setting timeLimit.
do: Estimate route length, then apply the multiplier
Leave it null for relaxed or family games
avoid: Limits based on running speed

title: Spectators see bodies, not the game
text: People watching from the side see players walk, turn, step and react, but not the virtual floor. Design moments with visible body language: a sidestep around a hazard, a pause at a checkpoint, arms raised at the portal. A screen with the leaderboard gives them the rest.
use_when: Any MR design with an audience.
do: Plan 1-2 visible body moments
Describe spectator_view honestly
avoid: Assuming spectators understand what the player sees

title: Put key moments on the spectator side
text: Find where people stand and place a hazard dodge and the finish portal on that side, 1.5-3 m from them and inside the edge margin. They then see faces and reactions instead of backs. The layout brief must say which side the spectators are on.
use_when: Placing the finish and highlight hazards.
do: Finish portal facing the audience
One hazard on the spectator side
avoid: Finish in the far corner
Key moments with the player's back to the crowd

title: Show the race leaderboard on a screen
text: A TV or projector with the live leaderboard turns watchers into fans and gives the queue a reason to stay. Place it where spectators and the queue can both see it, not where players in headsets walk toward it.
use_when: Races, events, classes, the Fortal court wall screen.
do: Put the screen beside the queue
Use nicknames or team names
avoid: Real names or personal data on screen

title: Let parents and friends cheer and call out hints
text: Spectators can shout left or one more. Design moments where a hint helps: a checkpoint behind a prop, a hazard the player has not noticed yet. This creates fellowship without any spectator task inside the area.
use_when: Family or friend groups watching.
do: Place one checkpoint so it is fun to call out
Mention cheering in spectator_plan
avoid: Spectators walking into the area to help

title: Never give spectators a task inside the play area
text: Anyone standing on the floor is a real obstacle that players cannot see as part of the game. Spectator roles stay outside the edge: cheering, watching the screen, choosing the next player.
use_when: Any design that involves spectators.
do: Keep spectator roles outside the boundary
avoid: A friend standing at a checkpoint
Spectators holding props on the floor
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Entertain the queue at events
text: At booths the queue is the next set of players and the crowd that draws others in. Show the leaderboard or a looping trailer on a screen and let the queue watch players react. A short 2-3 minute play keeps the wait short.
use_when: Events, booths and malls with a queue.
do: Leaderboard or trailer on a screen facing the queue
Keep plays short
avoid: A queue that faces a blank wall

title: Race or shared floor: pick by space and goal
text: In a race each player walks their own copy and sees a live leaderboard; in a shared floor players see each other's avatars. Races feel competitive, but players on the same real floor can still collide, so they need a large floor or players taking turns. Shared floor suits families and teamwork.
use_when: Choosing play_mode with more than one player.
do: Race on large floors or as turns
Shared floor for families and teamwork
avoid: Simultaneous races on a small floor

title: Cap players at once by area: about 8 square metres each
text: When several people share one real floor (a shared-floor game or a simultaneous race), each walking player needs about 6-10 square metres to move without bumping into others. Divide the floor area by 8 and round down, then cap at 6: a 4 x 5 m floor fits 2, a 7 x 7 m floor fits 6 on paper but 4 is safer with hazards to dodge. More people than that means turns, not a bigger group.
use_when: Setting group_size for a shared-floor or simultaneous MR game.
do: Divide the floor area by 8 square metres and round down
Lower the count if the route has many hazards
avoid: Filling the floor to the cap with kids who move unpredictably
Counting floor area that is inside the 0.6 m edge margin

title: Two mirrored lanes for a fair side-by-side race
text: On floors over about 8 m wide, split the floor into two mirrored lanes with at least a 1 m gap so two players race at once without crossing. Spectators love seeing them side by side, and mirrored lanes keep the race fair.
use_when: Two-player races in halls, courts or car parks.
do: Mirror the checkpoints exactly
Keep a 1 m buffer between lanes
avoid: Lanes that cross
Lanes on floors under 8 m wide

title: Turns plus an all-day leaderboard replace live races at busy events
text: When more people want to play than the floor can hold, let them play one or two at a time and compete on a leaderboard that runs all day. A player who finished can come back to see if they still lead, and the next player knows the score to beat before putting the headset on. Reset the board at a fixed time and announce the leader.
use_when: Events and classes with more players than space.
do: Run one leaderboard across the whole day
Tell each player the score to beat before they start
avoid: Holding people back to race everyone at once
Leaderboards with real names

title: Estimate throughput: players per hour
text: Players per hour = 60 / (play minutes + changeover minutes) x headsets. A 3 minute play with a 1.5 minute changeover on 2 headsets gives about 26 players per hour. Use this to set the play length the event can afford.
use_when: Event planning with a target number of players.
do: Ask how many people are expected
Shorten plays if throughput is too low
avoid: Ignoring changeover time

title: On PC skip every question about the real room
text: A PC game has no real floor, so do not ask about size, surroundings, obstacles or venue, and do not set venue, width_m, depth_m or indoor. Spend those questions on players, feelings and session instead.
use_when: The creator chooses platform pc.
do: Skip the environment questions
Ask more about players and feelings
avoid: Asking for floor size on PC

title: On PC, friends watch the screen, not the body
text: PC spectators see the same screen as the player, so they understand everything that happens. Loud visual feedback on hits, checkpoints and the finish makes watching fun, and hot-seat turns with a leaderboard work well for friends.
use_when: PC games played with friends nearby.
do: Make hits and checkpoints visually loud
Offer hot-seat turns
avoid: Designing body-language moments that only matter in MR

title: PC players expect WASD, mouse look and quick restarts
text: On PC the runner is played with WASD and battle uses a third person sword with a 3-hit combo and a dash. Players expect standard controls, instant restarts and tighter challenge than in MR, because nobody walks a real floor. Routes can be longer and hazards denser than in MR.
use_when: PC options and build.
do: Keep standard WASD and mouse
Tighten timing compared to MR
avoid: Copying MR walking time limits to PC
Custom control schemes

title: Ideas too intense for MR belong on PC
text: On PC nobody walks a real floor, so a fast pace, darker and scarier themes, dense hazards and dramatic heights are safe. When the creator wants something that breaks an MR safety rule (sprinting, jump scares, a long void walk), say why it is unsafe in a headset and offer PC as the home for that idea, or a gentle MR version alongside it.
use_when: The creator asks for speed, scares or heights that MR cannot do safely.
do: Explain the MR safety reason in one line
Offer the PC platform for the intense version
avoid: Porting intense PC ideas straight into MR
Refusing the idea without an alternative

title: Loud venues drown out game sound: make every cue visual
text: Events, malls, gyms and halls are loud, and music or a crowd covers headset audio. Any cue that matters (a hazard, the next checkpoint, the time running out) must also be visible: the red hazard circle, the checkpoint label, the timer. Treat sound as a bonus layer, and remember the crowd can be the soundtrack: cheering at the finish is part of the show.
use_when: Events, malls, gyms or anywhere with music or a crowd.
do: Make every important cue visible
Put the finish where the crowd can cheer
avoid: Story told only through audio
Warnings that are only a sound

title: Rain and wind outdoors need a covered fallback
text: Quest headsets are not waterproof, and wet grass or tiles become slippery. Wind blows hair into faces, moves loose decorations and can push light barriers onto the floor. For any outdoor plan ask about a covered fallback (a tent, a porch, an indoor room) and design a version of the Land that fits it.
use_when: Outdoor venues, especially in the rainy season.
do: Ask for a covered fallback space and its size
Keep loose barriers and banners well outside the floor
avoid: Playing in drizzle
Outdoor-only plans in the rainy season

title: The real floor surface changes how fast players can walk
text: Players feel the real floor under the virtual one. Smooth tiles and court floors allow a brisk walk; carpet is safe but rugs with edges catch feet; grass is uneven and slower; polished stone can be slippery in socks. Ask what the floor is, remove rugs and cables, and lengthen time limits on grass or carpet.
use_when: Any MR venue, before setting time limits and hazard density.
do: Ask what the floor surface is
Remove rugs and cables from the floor
Add time on grass or thick carpet
avoid: Tight time limits on grass
Playing in socks on polished floors

title: Low light, mirrors and glass walls can break headset tracking
text: The headset tracks itself with its cameras. Very dark rooms, large mirrors, glass walls, and plain featureless floors or walls can make it lose its place, so the virtual floor drifts or freezes. Keep the room moderately lit, cover big mirrors, and keep the route away from glass walls, which players also may not see in passthrough.
use_when: Dim venues, dance studios with mirrors, glass shopfronts or atriums.
do: Keep some room light on
Cover large mirrors
Keep 1 m or more from glass walls
avoid: Pitch dark spooky rooms
Routes along a mirror wall or glass shopfront
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Young kids play with a parent at the edge or as a second player
text: A child of 6-9 often wants a parent close. Either the parent stands at the edge as the spotter and calls out hints, or the parent wears a second headset and plays on a shared floor beside the child. A parent walking on the floor without a headset is a real obstacle the child may not expect, so avoid that.
use_when: Families with young children.
do: Offer a shared floor so a parent can play beside the child
Or put the parent at the edge as the spotter
avoid: A parent walking on the floor without a headset
Races between a parent and a small child on one floor

title: Wheelchair users in MR need wide turns and labels at seated eye height
text: A wheelchair needs about 1.5 m to turn around, so make the corridor at least 1.5 m wide and leave a 1.5 m circle at each checkpoint and at sharp turns. A seated player's eyes are about 1.2 m above the floor, so keep labels and targets low. Choose a smooth hard floor, no hazards that need side steps, and no void floor.
use_when: A wheelchair user will play in MR.
do: Make corridors and turns 1.5 m wide
Keep labels at seated eye height
Use a smooth hard floor
avoid: Hazards that need side steps
Thick carpet or grass
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Temples, schools and museums need respectful themes
text: In a temple ground, a school or a museum, the theme must fit the place: no ghosts or horror on temple grounds, no violence-themed battle in a primary school, quiet play near prayer halls or classrooms in session. Ask the host about rules on photos, shoes, sound and opening times, and lean on discovery and narrative themes that tell the place's own story.
use_when: Venues with cultural, religious or educational rules.
do: Ask the host about rules and quiet hours
Use the place's own story as the theme
avoid: Thai ghost themes on temple grounds
Loud play near prayer halls or classes

title: Stairs, stage edges and ponds near the floor need extra margin
text: The 0.6 m edge margin assumes a flat wall or open floor beyond the edge. If the floor ends at stairs, a stage edge, a pond, a pool or a balcony, keep everything at least 2 m away from that side and point the route away from it, because a player stepping backwards cannot see it.
use_when: The floor borders stairs, a stage edge, water or a drop.
do: Ask what is just beyond each edge
Keep 2 m from drops and water
avoid: Hazards that make players step back toward a drop
Finishing on a stage edge
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Give every player a 30 second safety briefing
text: Before the headset goes on, tell each player three things: walk, do not run; the boundary will appear if you get close to the edge; take the headset off or raise a hand to stop. At events the intro card can repeat walk, do not run in the rules list. It costs 30 seconds and prevents most accidents.
use_when: Events, classes and first-time players.
do: Brief walk-do-not-run, the boundary and how to stop
Repeat walk, do not run in the rules
avoid: Putting headsets on players with no briefing
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: At home, close the doors and keep pets and small children off the floor
text: In a living room the risks are not the walls but things that move: a dog, a toddler, a sibling walking through, a door that opens into the floor. Ask the creator to close doors, keep pets out and agree that nobody crosses the floor during play. Put the spawn on the side away from the door.
use_when: Home play in a living room or bedroom.
do: Close doors and keep pets out
Spawn away from the door
avoid: Routes that pass a door that opens inward
